scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The galop originated in the early 19th century in southwestern Germany as the Hopser or Rutscher.
It was introduced to Parisian society in the late 1820s by the Duchesse de Berry and became a fashionable ballroom dance in Vienna, Berlin, and London.
on_screen: Map: France, Germany, Austria · Europe
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The galop was frequently used as the final dance of the evening at balls, serving as an energetic conclusion to the night's festivities.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: File:Le galop de la girafe.webm (https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d5/Le_galop_de_la_girafe.webm?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=imageinfo&utm_content=original)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Couples dance in a closed position, moving rapidly across the floor.
The basic step combines a glissade with a chassé on alternate feet.
It is often performed in a circular path, sometimes involving a change of direction or position at the end of a series of eight steps.
Watch for Chassé.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (NZaeTPXlKAg)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Circular movement around the ballroom floor.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is written in a fast 2/4 meter.
Orchestral arrangements are common, often featuring the cornet, as exemplified by the 'Post Horn Galop.'
Listen for the Orchestra, Cornet, Piano.
The pulse is 2/4.

The music is characterized by a rapid, relentless 2/4 beat that drives the dancers forward. It features bright, staccato melodies and often incorporates brass instruments like the cornet to create a sense of urgency and excitement.
on_screen: Instrument names on screen as each is mentioned
Listen later: Post Horn Galop — Herman Koenig; Grand Galop Chromatique — Franz Liszt
Waveform or rhythm-pattern graphic: Rapid, driving pulse with a strong accent on the downbeat.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: In the 1820s, the dance influenced fashion, leading women to shorten their dresses to the ankle to accommodate the rapid sliding steps.
It was traditionally performed in ballrooms.

Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: Johann Strauss II, Franz Liszt, Hans Christian Lumbye, Herman Koenig, and the Duchesse de Berry.
Known as 'galopede' in Australian bush dance, 'Schnellpolka' in Germany, and historically as 'Hopser' or 'Rutscher' in Germany.
The galop is a direct precursor to the polka, which gained popularity in the 1830s.
